ledger.claim_text: The SR-71 Blackbird operational cruising altitude was approximately 85,000 feet at Mach 3.2 in the upper stratosphere, where a shockwave displacement of just one millimeter can choke the engines in milliseconds.
ledger.source_title: Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird Flight Manual (TO 1SR-71A-1) / NASA TM-86737
ledger.publisher: United States Air Force / NASA Dryden Flight Research Center
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Operational ceiling exceeded 85,000 ft with standard cruise speed between Mach 3.17 and Mach 3.2. Shockwave stability inside the mixed-compression inlet required sub-millimeter throat precision.

ledger.claim_text: The moveable inlet spike translates rearward by up to 26 inches (66 cm) inside the cowl at Mach 3 to trap conical shockwaves and decelerate supersonic airflow down to subsonic speeds (Mach 0.5) before the compressor face.
ledger.source_title: NASA Technical Note D-6397: Performance of an Axisymmetric Mixed-Compression Inlet at Mach 3
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: The translating spike moves mechanically back up to 26 inches depending on Mach number, capturing the normal shock in the diffuser throat and decelerating supersonic airflow to subsonic Mach 0.5.

ledger.claim_text: An inlet unstart occurs when internal pressure balance fails and the terminal normal shockwave is violently expelled forward out of the intake cowl in fifty milliseconds, causing sudden asymmetric thrust and high drag without an engine explosion.
ledger.source_title: NASA TM-86737: Flight Evaluation of an Inlet Unstart Detection and Recovery System on the SR-71
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Expulsion of the internal normal shock wave ('unstart') results in massive duct pressure surge within 50 ms, instantaneous loss of thrust, and huge nacelle drag. It is an aerodynamic flow expulsion, not a mechanical combustion explosion.

ledger.claim_text: The sudden asymmetric thrust and drag during an unstart produced violent yaw acceleration that slammed pilots wearing David Clark full-pressure suits against the cockpit canopy glass with sufficient force to crack or shatter flight helmets.
ledger.source_title: Sled Driver: Flying the World's Fastest Jet / Skunk Works Memoirs
ledger.publisher: Smithsonian Air & Space Magazine / Brian Shul & Rich Graham
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Pilots wearing David Clark S1030 pressure suits recounted violent head strikes against the canopy window during violent yaw unstarts before DAFICS digital control was introduced.

ledger.claim_text: At Mach 3.2 cruise, the Pratt & Whitney J58 turbo-ramjet's bypass bleed pipes converted the afterburner into a ramjet, with the intake diffuser and ejector nozzle generating approximately 80% of total forward thrust.
ledger.source_title: The J58 Engine and Its Bleed Bypass Design: Propulsion for the Blackbird
ledger.publisher: Aircraft Engine Historical Society / Pratt & Whitney Technical Heritage
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: At Mach 3.2, approximately 80% of total system thrust was generated by pressure recovery in the inlet diffuser and ejector nozzle, with the core turbojet acting primarily as a gas generator for the ramjet effect.

ledger.claim_text: Atmospheric skin friction heated the titanium airframe to over 600°F (with leading edges exceeding 800°F), expanding the fuselage by several inches in flight to seal fuel joints that leaked JP-7 on the ground.
ledger.source_title: Lockheed Skunk Works: A Personal Memoir of My Years at Lockheed / Ben R. Rich
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Fuselage expanded several inches in flight; JP-7 fuel tanks were designed without elastomeric bladders due to high temperatures, sealing as thermal expansion took up tolerances.

ledger.claim_text: Over approximately 4,000 surface-to-air missiles fired at the SR-71 during its active military service, zero aircraft were lost to enemy weapons, with tactical doctrine relying on high-altitude acceleration.
ledger.source_title: SR-71 Blackbird: Stories, Tales, and Legends / Paul F. Crickmore
ledger.publisher: National Museum of the United States Air Force / Osprey Publishing
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: USAF records confirm over 4,000 missile launches (including SA-2 and SA-5 systems) without a single loss to hostile fire.

ledger.claim_text: The SR-71 was officially retired by the USAF in 1998 and NASA in 1999, remaining the world's fastest and highest-flying air-breathing manned operational aircraft in history.
ledger.source_title: NASA Armstrong Fact Sheet: SR-71 Blackbird / National Air and Space Museum
ledger.publisher: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center & Smithsonian Institution
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: The SR-71 retains the official absolute speed record of 2,193.2 mph (3,529.6 km/h) set in July 1976 and sustained altitude record of 85,069 feet.
